title: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy successfully treated with mefloquine and literature review
case_prompt:
A 52-year-old man with a history of coronary stent placement and living-donor kidney transplantation (on prednisolone 5 mg daily and mycophenolate mofetil 360 mg twice daily) presented with a 2-week history of positional vertigo and a 3-day history of tinnitus, ear pressure, and left-ear hearing loss. He denied other neurologic complaints.  

On neurologic examination, Weber lateralized to the right, there was bilateral nasolabial-fold blunting, and truncal ataxia; other cranial nerves, motor, sensory, cerebellar testing, and otoscopic examination were unremarkable. The initial impression was multiple cranial nerve palsy.  

Brain MRI showed bilateral facial nerve enhancement (left > right) and subtle FLAIR hyperintensity with T1 hypointensity in the left temporal white matter. He was admitted with an initial diagnosis of Ramsay–Hunt syndrome and received intravenous dexamethasone, oral methylprednisolone, famciclovir, and intratympanic dexamethasone, which aggravated bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. He was then referred to neurology with the impression of encephalitis of infectious or autoimmune etiology.  

CSF examination showed 8 leukocytes/µL (75% lymphocytes), a normal protein level (39 mg/dL), and negative Gram stain, bacterial culture, and cryptococcal antigen. CSF PCR was positive for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and negative for mycobacteria, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, varicella zoster virus (VZV), and John Cunningham virus (JCV). Serum JCV PCR was positive. EBV viral capsid antigen IgG was positive, but IgM was negative.  

After 2 weeks of antiviral treatment, follow-up brain MRI demonstrated FLAIR hyperintensity and T1 hypointensity in the subcortical white matter of the left temporal lobe and dorsal pons, suggesting lymphoproliferative disease or progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. Whole-body PET revealed no abnormal hypermetabolism. An initial workup including ganglioside antibodies, antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, angiotensin-converting enzyme level, aquaporin-4 IgG, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein IgG, vitamin B12, and folate levels was normal.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Ramsay–Hunt syndrome was initially suspected due to facial nerve enhancement and ear symptoms — “with the initial impression of Ramsay-Hunt syndrome.”  
2. Viral encephalitis (VZV) was considered but excluded when CSF PCR returned negative for varicella zoster virus — “negative results for … varicella zoster virus (VZV).”  
3. CNS vasculitis was considered but excluded by a normal autoimmune and inflammatory workup — “an initial workup that included … antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody … showed that these levels were normal.”  
4. Lymphoproliferative disease was suspected based on MRI but excluded by absence of hypermetabolism on PET — “Whole-body positron emission tomography … revealed no abnormal hypermetabolism, which would suggest malignancy.”  
5. EBV infection was considered after positive CSF PCR but deemed unlikely to represent acute disease given serology — “EBV viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgG was positive, but EBV VCA IgM was negative.”  
6. PML was then suspected on the basis of immunosuppression, temporal white-matter lesions, and positive serum JCV PCR despite negative CSF JCV PCR — “clinical and imaging features supporting PML and was categorized as possible PML.”
